text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday hailed U.S. President Bill Clinton's victory and said his re-election would give a push to Middle East peace.
"I am very happy for the victory of a friend of the Palestinian people and a friend of peace," Arafat told reporters.

"I congratulate him and congratulate myself, the Palestinian people and the Arab nation for this victory which will bring stability and give a push to the peace process," Arafat said in the West Bank town of Ramallah.
Senior PLO officials also expressed the hope that Washington would move Middle East peace talks forward.

Israel and the PLO are locked in slow-moving negotiations on implementing an Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron. U.S.-sponsored Israeli-Syrian talks have been frozen since Moslem militant suicide bombings in February and March.
"We consider the victory of President Clinton a positive step towards a comprehensive, just and permanent peace in the Middle East," Palestinian Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei told Reuters.
"It is prime time that the U.S. plays an active role in the peace talks between Palestinians and Israelis and acts as a referee," Korei said.
Senior Palestinian peace negotiator Hassan Asfour said he hoped Clinton would press Israel to implement a long-overdue troop redeployment in Hebron.
"We hope that his coming administration will be more forceful," Asfour told Reuters.
U.S.-sponsored Israeli-PLO talks are deadlocked over implementation of the troop pullback in Hebron, home to 400 Jewish settlers and 100,000 Palestinians.
Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to renegotiate the Hebron deal signed by Israel's previous centre-left government.

Israel was due to redeploy troops in Hebron last March. The pullback was delayed by suicide bombings that killed 59 people. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants stronger security arrangements for the Jews in Hebron.
Israel's right-wing government has charged Palestinians were delaying a deal until after the American elections in the hopes of increasing U.S. pressure on the Jewish state.
Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he did not expect the Clinton administration to pressure Israel into peace concessions.
